title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: The Global Delivery Matrix, Billing Cycle, and the ₹100 Revenue Waterfall
question: How does Coforge source, staff, and deliver multi-year engineering contracts across 33 countries, and how much of every ₹100 billed actually converts into free cash flow?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is an opinion negotiated by sales; free cash flow is the physical truth settled by working capital.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Maxim

web_blocks.html: An IT firm's supply chain is not factories or freight. It is engineering talent, time-zone fit, delivery-center costs, and cash discipline. As of Q2 FY27, Coforge runs delivery hubs in 33 countries with 47,365 total staff [4, 19]. That headcount includes 34,628 IT billable staff and 10,024 BPS billable staff [4, 19]. For years, Indian IT exporters used a two-node model. They placed senior architects onsite in the US or Europe and ran large offshore teams in Noida, Pune, Hyderabad, and Bengaluru. In May 2026, the Encora deal added a third node: thousands of nearshore engineers in Colombia, Mexico, Costa Rica, and Brazil [6]. Those teams work directly in US time zones [6].

This tri-shore model splits Q2 FY27 IT sales into 49.5% onsite and 50.5% offshore India, including SLK Global's Tier-3 hubs [10, 19]. Adding LatAm nearshore lifted the reported onsite share from 47.7% in Q2 FY26 to 49.5% in Q2 FY27 [10, 19]. Nearshore LatAm work earns higher billing rates than India offshore while costing less than US onshore engineers [6]. That lets Coforge staff agile product pods for Silicon Valley and Fortune 500 clients while protecting gross margin [6]. On sales, client partners mine top accounts, where Top 5 clients give 18.1% and Top 10 give 26.4% of Q2 FY27 sales [5, 19]. A separate large-deal team chases $20M–$230M multi-year contracts [5, 19].

web_blocks.takeaway: Coforge's tri-shore delivery model (India offshore + Tier-3 BPM + LatAm nearshore + US/UK onsite) supports ~82.4% utilization and 10.4% attrition while reducing top-5 client concentration to 18.1%.

web_blocks.html: IT unit economics rest on two drivers: utilization-adjusted gross margin and the cash collection cycle. In fixed-price deals, firms book sales as project milestones are met [1, 22]. That creates unbilled revenue until the client signs off and an invoice goes out [1, 22]. Once billed, standard enterprise payment terms run 60 to 90 days. Screener data shows Coforge's annual Debtor Days rose from 73 days in FY23 and FY24 to 78 days in FY25 and 88 days in FY26, while Working Capital Days climbed from 13 in FY23 to 25 in FY26 [1]. More importantly, Q2 FY27 disclosures reveal that Total DSO (including billed receivables, unbilled revenue, and contract assets) stretched a further 8 days sequentially to 110 days—split into 65 billed days, 26 unbilled days, and 19 contract-asset days—as net unbilled revenue jumped from ₹2,100 Cr to ₹2,600 Cr. Management attributed this unbilled build-up to invoicing and collection lags while migrating contracts from Encora's US entity to India under legal-entity rationalization; shrinking Total DSO back down is now the single highest-priority working-capital watchpoint.

Two cross-border policy and currency mechanics also shape unit profitability. First, on US immigration policy, Coforge derives roughly 55% of revenue from the US—meaningfully below mid-cap peers such as Persistent Systems, LTIMindtree, and Mphasis at 75%–80%—and Encora's Latin American nearshore hubs buffer Coforge against the $100,000 new US H-1B visa fee (which broker estimates place at a theoretical 50–150 bps industry margin drag if fully absorbed, and materially lower in practice). Second, on foreign exchange, legacy forward hedges generated $10.2 million of FX hedge losses in Q2 FY27 (similar to Q1 FY27), weighing on non-operating income; management expects hedge losses to taper to $7.1–7.5 million in Q3 FY27 and $1.2 million in Q4 FY27 before dropping to zero thereafter, aided by the natural hedge of its $550 million USD term loan.

To trace how revenue turns into cash, we build a ₹100 Revenue-to-FCF waterfall from FY26 audited results [1]. Screener groups FY26 staff pay, subcontractor fees, and operating costs into one ₹13,467 Cr expense line [1]. That leaves ₹2,936 Cr in Operating EBITDA, or a 17.9% margin [1]. Upfront deal bonuses on large contracts are also amortized inside staff expenses over the contract life [22].

web_blocks.caption: COFORGE: Worked ₹100 Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall (Audited FY26 / Mar 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every ₹100 of audited FY26 revenue (₹16,403 Cr total), Coforge generated ₹17.90 in operating EBITDA, ₹10.64 in reported PAT (aided by a 13% effective tax rate), ₹10.92 in operating cash flow, and ₹7.30 in Free Cash Flow after ₹3.63 of capex [1].

web_blocks.title: Why FY26 Free Cash Flow Lagged the 10-Year Peak
paragraphs: The waterfall shows a clear dip in cash conversion. In FY25, Coforge turned 96% of pre-tax EBITDA into operating cash flow, but in FY26 that ratio fell to 76% [1]. Two factors caused the drop. First, Debtor Days stretched from 78 to 88 days as large project milestones scaled [1, 3]. Second, capital spending rose to ₹595 Cr (3.6% of sales) for global hubs and AI tools [1, 3]. Investors should watch if debtor days return to 73–78 days after Encora.

book_paragraphs: To understand whether an IT services business is a genuine cash machine or an accounting mirage, you and I have to follow two trails: how it staffs and prices its engineers across time zones, and how cleanly ₹100 of billed revenue turns into ₹100 of spendable cash.

Coforge's delivery supply chain today looks radically different from the classic Indian offshore shop of ten years ago. With 47,365 employees across 33 countries—34,628 in IT services and 10,024 in Business Process Solutions—management runs a tri-shore model. Roughly 49.5% of IT revenue is delivered onsite near the client, while 50.5% is delivered offshore, increasingly blended with Latin American nearshore engineers from the May 2026 Encora acquisition and Tier-3 Indian delivery centers inherited from SLK Global.

book_subsections.title: Tri-Shore Geometry, Utilization, and the Talent Pyramid
paragraphs: Why does that tri-shore geometry matter? Because North American software and banking clients increasingly demand agile product teams working in their own time zones, yet balk at paying $150-an-hour onshore rates for an entire pod. By pairing US architects with Colombian, Mexican, or Brazilian nearshore developers and Indian offshore automation teams, Coforge achieves an average revenue per employee near $70,000 while defending an 82.4% utilization rate and an enviable 10.4% LTM attrition rate.

Low attrition is a quiet profit engine in services. Every percentage point of attrition avoided saves lateral-hiring premiums, onboarding bench time, and client rework. Meanwhile, Coforge's go-to-market engine balances deep account mining with diversification: Top 5 clients accounted for 18.1% of Q2 FY27 revenue (down from 21.0% a year earlier even as those top five accounts grew 20.4% year-on-year), while Top 10 clients represented 26.4%. That means no single customer holds Coforge hostage, yet large accounts continue to compound.

book_subsections.title: Walking Down the Audited FY26 ₹100 Revenue Waterfall
paragraphs: Now walk down the audited FY26 ₹100 waterfall with me. Out of every ₹100 of consolidated revenue (₹16,403 Cr total), ₹82.10 goes to operating expenses—mostly engineering payroll, subcontractors, ESOPs, and SG&A—leaving ₹17.90 in operating EBITDA (₹2,936 Cr). Subtract ₹4.16 for depreciation and amortization (₹682 Cr, stepped up after Cigniti), ₹1.03 for interest (₹169 Cr), and ₹0.51 for net non-operating charges (-₹83 Cr), and you arrive at ₹12.21 in pre-tax profit (₹2,003 Cr).

Because FY26 benefited from a one-time non-cash Deferred Tax Liability reversal from the Cigniti merger, income taxes took only ₹1.57 (₹258 Cr, a 13% effective rate), leaving ₹10.64 in reported net profit (₹1,745 Cr). Here is the forensic catch we must respect: working capital absorbed cash in FY26 as debtor days stretched from 78 to 88 days, pulling Working Capital Days from 18 to 25. Operating cash flow came in at ₹10.92 per ₹100 of revenue (₹1,792 Cr total), and after ₹3.63 of capital expenditure (₹595 Cr), Free Cash Flow settled at ₹7.30 per ₹100 of sales (₹1,197 Cr). That is still solidly cash-generative, but it reminds us that milestone billing and M&A integration can temporarily trap cash in receivables.

callouts.title: The 80-Day DSO Rule of Thumb
callouts.text: In mid-tier IT services, debtor days in the 70–78 day range represent normal enterprise billing cadence. Whenever DSO pushes toward 88–90+ days, you must check whether unbilled milestone revenue is piling up faster than client cash collections.

book_subsections.title: Tracing Every ₹100 Through the FY26 P&L and Cash Flow Waterfall
paragraphs: Numbers on a spreadsheet only come alive when you trace a single ₹100 note from the moment a client signs an invoice to the cash left over in Coforge's bank account. Using our audited FY26 (March 2026) waterfall, out of every ₹100 of consolidated revenue (₹16,403 Cr total), direct delivery and employee compensation consumed roughly ₹62.40, while other operating, G&A, and subcontracting expenses took ₹19.70—leaving ₹17.90 in operating EBITDA (₹2,936 Cr).

From that ₹17.90 of EBITDA, depreciation and amortization absorbed ₹4.20, net interest expense took ₹0.90, other income added back ₹0.60, and corporate taxes claimed ₹2.80, leaving ₹10.60 in net profit (PAT of ₹1,745 Cr). Now here is the forensic check you must never skip: did that ₹10.60 of accounting profit actually arrive in cash? In FY26, cash flow from operations (CFO) was ₹10.90 per ₹100 of revenue (₹1,792 Cr, or 76% of EBITDA before working-capital timing), and capital expenditure absorbed ₹3.60 per ₹100 (₹595 Cr), leaving ₹7.30 of true Free Cash Flow per ₹100 of revenue (₹1,197 Cr). Understanding that gap between ₹17.90 EBITDA and ₹7.30 FCF explains why working-capital discipline and debtor days are central to our ongoing monitoring.

book_subsections.title: Delivery Mix, Subcontracting, H-1B Policy & Why Total DSO Hit 110 Days
paragraphs: Understanding Coforge's unit economics also requires looking at its delivery geography, policy exposure, and billing cycle. Historically, Coforge has maintained a balanced onshore-offshore mix, with roughly half of revenue delivered from offshore Indian campuses (Greater Noida, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Pune, Mumbai) and half onshore or nearshore close to client headquarters. With Encora's LatAm hubs in Mexico, Costa Rica, and Brazil now inside the tent—and US revenue representing roughly 55% of the mix versus 75%–80% at mid-cap peers like Persistent Systems, LTIMindtree, and Mphasis—Coforge is better insulated against the $100,000 new US H-1B visa fee while pitching a three-timezone 'follow-the-sun' engineering model to Fortune 500 CTOs.

The sharper friction sits in working capital and legacy FX hedges. After FY26 annual debtor days stretched to 88 days, Q2 FY27 disclosures showed Total DSO (including billed receivables, unbilled revenue, and contract assets) rising another 8 days sequentially to 110 days—composed of 65 billed days, 26 unbilled days, and 19 contract-asset days—as net unbilled revenue climbed from ₹2,100 Cr to ₹2,600 Cr during the legal-entity migration of Encora's US contracts to India. Meanwhile, legacy forward hedges produced $10.2 million of FX hedge losses in Q2 FY27, though management expects those losses to taper to $7.1–7.5 million in Q3 FY27, $1.2 million in Q4 FY27, and zero thereafter as the $550 million USD term loan provides a natural balance-sheet hedge. Reversing that unbilled build-up is the fastest way to unlock trapped cash.

book_callouts.title: Watch the Post-Encora Cash Bridge
book_callouts.text: FY26's 76% CFO-to-EBITDA conversion stepped down from 96% in FY25, and Q2 FY27 Total DSO stretched to 110 days (₹2,600 Cr net unbilled) during Encora contract novation. Although H1 FY27 FCF-to-PAT improved to 92%, pulling Total DSO down as legal-entity migration completes is non-negotiable with $550 million of term debt on the books.
